title: Hard exam 6
about: Ten single-choice questions with traps: functions that change globals, a file truncated before it is read, variables set only for one command, double spaces and the difference between a builtin and its twin program.

questions.title: return and exit in functions
questions.text:
`s.sh` contains:
```
x=1
f() { x=2; return 5; echo never; }
f
echo "$? $x"
g() { exit 7; }
g
echo after
```
You run `bash s.sh; echo $?`. What is printed?

options.why: A function can change the variables of the script, and `exit 7` ends the whole script, not only the function.
`exit` inside a function ends the script, so `after` never appears.
`return 5` leaves `f` with status 5, and `x` is a global variable that `f` changed; `exit 7` in `g` ends the script with 7.
After `f`, `$?` holds the status given to `return`, 5.

questions.title: Sorting a file onto itself
questions.text: `f` contains the lines `c`, `a` and `b`. After `sort f > f`, what does `f` contain?

options.why: The sort result is never written: the file is emptied before `sort` runs.
`>` replaces the content, it does not add to it.
The shell opens `f` for writing, truncating it, before `sort` starts, so `sort` reads an empty file.

options.t: The shell refuses to run the command, because input and output are the same file.
options.why: The shell does not check that; the data are simply lost.

questions.title: The current job
questions.text: You run `sleep 100 &`, which becomes job 1. Then you run `sleep 200` in the foreground and press Ctrl+Z, which makes it job 2. You type `bg` with no argument. What happens?

options.t: Job 1 is resumed in the background, because it was the first job created.
options.why: It is already running in the background.

options.t: Job 2 resumes in the background: it is the current job.
options.why: Without a job number, `bg` acts on the current job, the one that was most recently stopped.

options.t: Both jobs are placed in the foreground, one after the other.
options.why: `bg` never uses the foreground.

options.t: An error message, since `bg` always needs a job number as its argument.
options.why: The job number is optional.

questions.title: A variable set for one command only
questions.text:
What do these lines print?
```
a=1; b=$a; a=2
a=3 echo $a ${b}0
echo $a
```

options.why: `$a` in the second line is expanded by the shell before `a=3` takes effect, and the prefix applies only to that command.
`${b}0` is the value of `b` followed by 0; `b` was set to 1.
`a=3` is set only in the environment of `echo`, after `$a` has been replaced by 2; `b` kept the old value 1.
`b` was a copy of the old `a`, which was 1.

questions.title: Capital letters in a path
questions.text: A student types `mkdir Reports; cp data.txt reports/` and gets an error. What is wrong?

options.t: `cp` cannot copy into a directory that has just been created by `mkdir`.
options.why: A new directory can be used at once.

options.t: `Reports` and `reports` differ, as Linux names are case-sensitive.
options.why: `reports/` does not exist, so `cp` cannot copy into it.

options.t: The trailing slash in `reports/` is not allowed as an argument of `cp`.
options.why: The slash is fine when the name is a directory.

options.t: `mkdir` creates directory names in lower case only, whatever is typed.
options.why: It keeps the case that is typed.

questions.title: Two spaces
questions.text: What does `echo 'a  b c' | cut -d' ' -f2` print? (There are two spaces between `a` and `b`.)

options.why: Each space is a delimiter, so there is an empty field between the two spaces.
Field 1 is `a`; field 2 comes after the first space.
The fields are `a`, an empty one, `b` and `c`; field 2 is the empty one.
`cut` does not join fields: it selects one.

questions.title: Every two hours
questions.text: Which `crontab` entry runs `/opt/sync.sh` once every two hours, at minute 30?

options.why: The first field is the minute: it runs every two minutes.
The minute is `*`, so it runs every minute of the even hours 0, 2, 4, ... 22.
Minute 30 of every hour that is a multiple of two.
It runs once a day, at 02:30.

questions.title: Builtin and program with the same name
questions.text: `/bin/echo` exists as a program and bash also has a builtin `echo`. What do `echo --version` and `/bin/echo --version` print?

options.t: Both print the version of the `echo` program.
options.why: The builtin has no `--version` option and prints it as text.
The program in `/bin` accepts the option and shows its version.

options.t: The first prints `--version`; the second prints the version of the `echo` program.
options.why: Without a path, bash uses its builtin; with a path, it runs the program.

options.t: The first prints the version, and the second prints the text `--version`.
options.why: It is the other way round.

questions.title: Lines that are exactly a word
questions.text: `w` contains `end`, `endless`, `the end`, `end of file` and `bend`. A student wants only the line that is exactly `end`. Which command does it?

options.why: It also matches `endless` and `end of file`, which start with `end`.
It also matches `the end` and `bend`, which finish with `end`.
Whole word, but also in `the end` and `end of file`.
The line must start and finish with `end`, so nothing else can be on it.

questions.title: enable is not start
questions.text: `cups` is stopped and disabled. The administrator runs `systemctl enable cups` and then reboots the machine. Which statement is TRUE?

options.why: `enable` only registers the service for the next boots.

options.t: `cups` will not run after the reboot until `systemctl start cups` is run.
options.why: A service that is enabled is started by the boot sequence.

options.t: `cups` is still stopped right after `enable`, and it is running after the reboot.
options.why: `enable` adds it to the boot; `start` is what launches it now.

options.t: `cups` is running right after `enable` and will also be after the reboot.
options.why: Only the second part is true.
